description:
APK is an archive format used for distributing Android apps. It is based on the Jar format (for Java), and like that format, is actually a ZIP archive with a different extension, and with specific files and directories within it.

The executable part of the app is usually in either Dalvik Executable (for older Android versions prior to 5.0) or ART format (for newer versions).

description:
PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) is an encryption program, and its encryption format which eventually became the OpenPGP standard.

Created by Phil Zimmerman in 1991, it got into some legal trouble early on because encryption of this grade was classified as a munition under U.S. law and restricted from export. These laws, while not completely repealed even now, have been considerably liberalized since, and now export of PGP and related software is only restricted when it's being exported to countries such as Iran that are under special sanction. Zimmerman's PGP company was eventually acquired by Network Associates (now McAfee), which eventually rebranded the original command-line-based PGP as "McAfee E-Business Server" and sold off all other PGP assets to some PGP developers who formed a new PGP company, which was eventually acquired by Symantec. Meanwhile, the specifications of the file format had been released as the OpenPGP spec and published as an RFC document, making it available for use in other products.

GNU Privacy Guard (GnuPG, GPG) is a commonly-used encryption tool using PGP format, running on Linux systems.

PGP uses a combination of several encryption techniques applied serially, including symmetric-key and public-key cryptography.

name: video/h264
description:
Advanced Video Coding (AVC), also referred to as H.264 or MPEG-4 Part 10, Advanced Video Coding (MPEG-4 AVC), is a video compression standard based on block-oriented, motion-compensated integer-DCT coding.[1] It is by far the most commonly used format for the recording, compression, and distribution of video content, used by 91% of video industry developers as of September 2019.

It supports resolutions up to and including 8K UHD.

H.264 is controversial for being patent-encumbered, and hence subject to royalty requirements. In 2013, Cisco is attempting to partially remedy this by producing a freely distributed executable H.264 codec for many platforms for which they have paid the royalty, allowing anybody to download and use it in unmodified form royalty-free. The source code is also openly available, but any altered versions that anybody might create from it would require separate licensing, as would any distribution of the executables other than direct download from Cisco. Thus, the only way to use it as part of a product without additional license fees is to have the product's installer download the executable from Cisco during the install process, rather than including it directly in your own product (whether on disk or downloadable from your site).

HEVC (H.265) has been developed as a more efficient successor to this format, but it is also patent-encumbered. Attempts to create a royalty-free alternative include AV1, Daala, VP9, and Thor.

The H.264 specification does not, in an extremely strict sense, define a codec which fits into a series of bytes; instead, it describes the stream as fitting into a sequence of frames called "network abstraction layer units", which can then be delineated into a raw byte format by the user. The format for putting these into a raw bytestream described by Annex B of the specification apparently is apparently very widely-used.

JavaScript was originally developed at Netscape by Brendan Eich (who later became Mozilla CEO... very briefly), where it was originally called LiveScript while under development, but became JavaScript (with the name licensed from Sun) in order to capitalize on the popularity of Java, though the languages aren't really related (although there are some similarities in syntax). description:
MP3 is the name commonly given to the audio formats specified by MPEG-1 Layer III and MPEG-2 Layer III, standardized as ISO/IEC 11172-3:1993, with some additions in ISO/IEC 13818-3:1995. It uses lossy compressed data.

MP3 is based in part on work by the Fraunhofer Institute, which held patents in the format. Other companies may also have held patents encumbering its implementation. One of the relevant patents was [U.S. Patent 5,812,672](http://www.google.com/patents/US5812672), which expired in September 2015; many other related patents in various countries expired earlier. The final expiration of all relevant patents took until 2017, however, due to some "submarine patents" which were kept in the application process for years, extending their expiration dates. A modified version of DCT compression (Discrete cosine transform) is used, a lossy compression method also used in [JPEG images](/image/jpeg).

description: ORF, or Olympus RAW, is a raw image format produced by Olympus digital cameras. The format is TIFF-like, but with a different file signature. The full-size image is in the first IFD. There is also Exif data, with a MakerNote.

furtherReading.title: Let's Solve the File Format Problem!

name: image/x-pentax-pef
description: Pentax PEF (or Pentax RAW) is a raw image format associated with Pentax digital cameras. It is based on TIFF.

furtherReading.title: Let's Solve the File Format Problem!

name: image/x-fuji-raf
description: RAF, or Fujifilm RAW, is a raw image format used by some Fujifilm digital cameras.

furtherReading.title: Let's Solve the File Format Problem!

name: image/x-panasonic-raw
description:
Panasonic RAW/RW2, also known as Leica RAW or RWL, is a raw image format used by some Panasonic and Leica digital cameras. It can also be known by a camera-specific name such as Lumix RAW or Panasonic LX3 RAW.

Different cameras produce different versions of it, and at some point the .raw file extension was changed to .rw2. The term Panasonic RAW might refer to just the .raw files, but more likely includes both .raw and .rw2.

furtherReading.title: Let's Solve the File Format Problem!

name: audio/flac
description:
FLAC stands for Free Lossless Audio Codec, an audio format similar to MP3, but lossless, meaning that audio is compressed in FLAC without any loss in quality.

It can encode audio with a PCM bit resolution up to 32 bits per sample and sampling rates up to 640 kHz. FLAC-encoded audio is usually found either in a native container (which has the extension .flac), or in an Ogg container (when it's known as OggFLAC).

furtherReading.title: Let's Solve the File Format Problem!

name: image/x-sony-sr2
description: SR2 is a raw image format produced by some makes of Sony cameras. The format is based upon TIFF.

name: image/x-sigma-x3f
description: X3F (or Sigma X3F, or Foveon X3F) is a raw image format used by some Sigma digital cameras that use a "Foveon sensor".

furtherReading.title: Let's Solve the File Format Problem!

name: application/flowfile
description: The Apache NiFi FlowFile serialization formats are used within the NiFi project to serialize the FlowFile attributes and content of files leaving a NiFi instance. The serialization format referenced by this mimetype is distinct from the way FlowFiles are stored internally within NiFi.

name: application/flowfile-v1
description: The Apache NiFi FlowFile serialization version 1 format is used within the NiFi project to serialize the FlowFile attributes and content of files leaving a NiFi instance. The serialization format referenced by this mimetype is distinct from the way FlowFiles are stored internally within NiFi.

name: application/flowfile-v2
description: The Apache NiFi FlowFile serialization version 2 format is used within the NiFi project to serialize the FlowFile attributes and content of files leaving a NiFi instance. The serialization format referenced by this mimetype is distinct from the way FlowFiles are stored internally within NiFi.

name: application/flowfile-v3
description: The Apache NiFi FlowFile serialization version 3 format is used within the NiFi project to serialize the FlowFile attributes and content of files leaving a NiFi instance. The serialization format referenced by this mimetype is distinct from the way FlowFiles are stored internally within NiFi.

name: image/heif
description:
HEIF is the container format defined by MPEG-H Part 12 (ISO/IEC 23008-12) for still images and image sequences. A file is labelled image/heif when it conforms to the generic 'mif1' brand rather than committing to a particular codec, so the picture inside may be coded with HEVC or something else entirely.

Most people meet the format through Apple devices, but those photos are usually labelled [image/heic](/image/heic) instead, because they specifically use HEVC coding. If you are unsure which label applies, image/heif is the safer, more general one.

name: image/heic-sequence
description:
A HEIF container holding more than one HEVC-coded image, such as a burst, an animation, or the moving part of an Apple Live Photo. It uses the same container as [image/heic](/image/heic), but the separate label tells a reader to expect a series of timed images rather than a single still.

This is the type the `file` command reports for Live Stickers and similar `.heics` files, and the value you need in an HTML file input's `accept` attribute if you want to receive them.

name: image/heif-sequence
description:
The codec-agnostic counterpart to [image/heic-sequence](/image/heic-sequence): a HEIF container holding several coded images without committing to HEVC in particular.

Tools disagree about which of the two to report for the same file, so it is worth accepting both. On Linux the `file` command tends to say image/heif-sequence where a browser file input expects image/heic-sequence.

name: model/stl
description:
STL describes the surface of a three-dimensional object as a mesh of triangles. It carries no colour, no texture and no units, which is both why it is so simple to write and why so much information is lost on the way out of a CAD package.

It originated with 3D Systems' stereolithography machines in the late 1980s and became the common currency between modelling software and 3D printers, so nearly every slicer accepts it. Two layouts share the extension: a human-readable ASCII form and a much smaller binary form.

Watch out for the extension clash: [application/vnd.ms-pki.stl](/application/vnd.ms-pki.stl) is a Microsoft Certificate Trust List and has nothing to do with 3D models, despite also using `.stl`.

name: application/vnd.ms-outlook
description:
A single Outlook item saved out as a standalone file: an email, an appointment, a contact or a task. Internally it is a Microsoft Compound File Binary container holding the item's MAPI properties, so unlike a `.eml` file it preserves Outlook-specific fields instead of following the RFC 5322 message format.

This type is not registered with IANA, but it is what Microsoft's own documentation uses and what e-discovery and archiving tools consistently expect. You may also see the generic [application/octet-stream](/application/octet-stream) in the wild when a server has no mapping for the extension.

furtherReading.title: Library of Congress - Microsoft Outlook Item (MSG)
Microsoft Learn - Supported file types in eDiscovery

name: application/x-ipynb+json
description:
A Jupyter notebook: a JSON document holding an ordered list of cells containing code, prose and the output produced by running that code, plus metadata naming the kernel needed to execute it.

There is no registered media type for the format. application/x-ipynb+json is the unregistered name that Jupyter's own tooling and most editors settled on, so it is a community convention rather than a standard. If you know of an authoritative source that pins this down, the maintainers would welcome it.

name: application/x-ms-shortcut
description:
A Windows shortcut. It is a small binary file that points at something else — a program, a document, a folder, a drive or a network location — and carries the details Windows needs to open it, such as the working directory, any command line arguments, an icon to display, and enough information about the target to go looking for it if it has since moved.

Windows has used the format since Windows 95, where it replaced the older Program Information Files, and Microsoft documents it as the Shell Link Binary File Format. The type is not registered with IANA; `application/x-ms-shortcut` comes from the media type list shipped with the Apache HTTP Server and is the spelling that stuck.

One thing worth knowing if you are accepting these from users: because a shortcut can carry arguments and borrow its icon from an unrelated file, a `.lnk` can be made to look harmless while pointing somewhere else entirely. They have a long history as a malware delivery route, so treat unexpected ones with care.

furtherReading.title: Library of Congress - Microsoft Windows Shortcut File

name: image/jp2
description:
JP2 is the file format defined by JPEG 2000 Part 1 (ISO/IEC 15444-1) and registered by RFC 3745. It wraps a wavelet-coded image in a sequence of boxes carrying colour space, resolution and metadata alongside the picture data, so a decoder knows how to interpret the pixels without anything told to it out of band.

Wavelet coding gives it two properties JPEG lacks: genuinely lossless compression, and a codestream that can be truncated to yield a smaller or lower-quality image without re-encoding. That made it the format of choice for digital cinema distribution and for large-scale archival scanning at national libraries.

If your file is a bare codestream with no boxes around it, the right label is [image/j2c](/image/j2c).

furtherReading.title: RFC 3745 - MIME Type Registrations for JPEG 2000

name: image/jpx
description:
JPX is the extended file format from JPEG 2000 Part 2 (ISO/IEC 15444-2), registered alongside JP2 in RFC 3745. It uses the same box structure as [image/jp2](/image/jp2) but lifts its restrictions: multiple codestreams in one file, colour spaces beyond sRGB and greyscale, compositing instructions and richer metadata.

RFC 3745 registers `.jpf` for it. You will also meet `.jpx` in the wild, which is the same format under a more obvious name.

A file that only uses Part 1 features should be labelled image/jp2. JPX is for the ones that genuinely need the extensions.

furtherReading.title: RFC 3745 - MIME Type Registrations for JPEG 2000

name: image/jpm
description:
JPM is the compound image format from JPEG 2000 Part 6 (ISO/IEC 15444-6), registered by RFC 3745. It stores a page under a mixed raster content model: a low-resolution background layer, a high-resolution binary mask for text and line art, and a foreground colour layer.

Splitting a scanned page that way lets each layer use the compression that suits it, which is why JPM turns up in document capture and archiving systems rather than in general photography.

Both `.jpm` and `.jpgm` are registered for it.

furtherReading.title: RFC 3745 - MIME Type Registrations for JPEG 2000

name: image/j2c
description:
A bare JPEG 2000 codestream, with none of the boxes that make up a [image/jp2](/image/jp2) file. It is the raw output of the Part 1 (ISO/IEC 15444-1) encoder: entropy-coded wavelet data plus the markers a decoder needs, and nothing describing colour space or metadata.

You meet it embedded inside other containers — DICOM images, MXF video, PDF — where the wrapper already carries that information and a second copy would be redundant.

IANA registers no file extension for this type. `.j2c` and `.j2k` are both conventional and both common, and neither is official.

name: image/jph
description:
JPH is the file format for High-Throughput JPEG 2000, defined in ISO/IEC 15444-15. It keeps the box structure and the wavelet transform of [image/jp2](/image/jp2), and replaces only the block coder with one roughly an order of magnitude faster in both directions.

The trade is a small loss of compression efficiency in exchange for encode and decode speeds that make JPEG 2000 practical in live and interactive workflows rather than only archival ones. The codestream is not backwards compatible, so existing JP2 tooling needs updating to read it.

The bare codestream form, without the boxes, is [image/jphc](/image/jphc).

name: image/jphc
description:
A bare High-Throughput JPEG 2000 codestream (ISO/IEC 15444-15), standing in the same relation to [image/jph](/image/jph) as [image/j2c](/image/j2c) does to [image/jp2](/image/jp2): the coded data and its markers, without the boxes that carry colour space and metadata.

Use it where the surrounding container already describes the image and only the pixels are needed.

The registered extension is `.jhc`, not `.jphc`, which catches people out.

name: image/jxl
description:
JPEG XL (ISO/IEC 18181) is a still and animated image format built around a new codec, with one capability its neighbours lack: it can losslessly re-encode an existing JPEG file, typically around 20% smaller, and reconstruct the original bit for bit.

It also offers progressive decoding, lossless and lossy modes in a single codestream, wide colour gamut, high bit depth, transparency and animation — roughly the union of what [image/jpeg](/image/jpeg), [image/png](/image/png) and [image/webp](/image/webp) each do separately.

Adoption, not the technology, has been the sticking point. Check current browser support before serving it without a fallback.

name: image/jxr
description:
JPEG XR (ITU-T T.832, also published as ISO/IEC 29199-2) is a still image codec supporting lossy and lossless compression, high dynamic range and bit depths up to 32 bits per channel, at a computational cost close to ordinary JPEG.

It began at Microsoft as Windows Media Photo and was renamed HD Photo before standardisation, which is why `.wdp` files and the unregistered `image/vnd.ms-photo` label describe the same format.

Outside Microsoft's own stack it never displaced [image/jpeg](/image/jpeg), and support today is sparse.

name: image/jls
description:
JPEG-LS (ITU-T T.87, also ISO/IEC 14495-1) is a lossless and near-lossless still image codec based on the LOCO-I algorithm. Despite the name it shares little with baseline JPEG: it uses prediction and context modelling rather than a discrete cosine transform.

Near-lossless mode is the distinctive part. You set a maximum permitted error per sample and the encoder guarantees no pixel deviates by more than that — a bounded, inspectable loss rather than an open-ended one. Medical imaging adopted it for exactly that reason, and DICOM defines transfer syntaxes for it.

It is fast and simple to implement, which keeps it in use in embedded and scientific capture despite newer options.

name: image/apng
description:
APNG extends PNG with animation: a control chunk plus a sequence of frame chunks, all placed in chunk types a plain PNG decoder is required to skip. The first frame is a complete, valid PNG image, so software that does not understand APNG shows a still picture rather than failing.

That backwards compatibility is why it displaced GIF for short loops on the web — full 8-bit alpha and 24-bit colour instead of a 256-colour palette and 1-bit transparency.

It began as a Mozilla extension and was later registered with IANA and folded into the W3C PNG specification proper. The older Mozilla-era label is at [image/vnd.mozilla.apng](/image/vnd.mozilla.apng).

name: image/jxs
description:
JPEG XS (ISO/IEC 21122) is a low-latency, visually lossless codec designed around the opposite trade to most: it compresses only modestly, but does so in a fraction of a frame, with end-to-end latency measured in scanlines rather than frames.

That makes it a mezzanine format rather than a delivery one. It carries near-uncompressed video over links that cannot quite take raw pixels, which is how it ended up in SMPTE ST 2110-22 for professional video over IP, with RFC 9134 defining the RTP payload format.

`image/jxs` labels the file form; the bare codestream is [image/jxsc](/image/jxsc).

furtherReading.title: RFC 9134 - RTP Payload Format for ISO/IEC 21122 (JPEG XS)

name: image/jxsc
description:
A bare JPEG XS codestream (ISO/IEC 21122), without the file structure that [image/jxs](/image/jxs) provides. It is what travels over the wire on a professional video-over-IP link, where the transport already carries timing and format information.

The IANA registry lists further JPEG XS types for carriage inside ISO base media containers, which this site does not document yet.

name: image/avci
description:
AVCI is a still image coded with AVC (H.264) and stored in the HEIF container defined by ISO/IEC 23008-12 — the same container as [image/heif](/image/heif) and [image/heic](/image/heic), but committing to AVC rather than HEVC.

It exists because HEIF's container design is deliberately codec-agnostic, and the media type is how a file declares which codec is actually inside. In practice it is far rarer than HEIC, since the devices that adopted HEIF adopted HEVC along with it.

The image sequence form is [image/avcs](/image/avcs).

name: image/avcs
description:
The image sequence counterpart to [image/avci](/image/avci): several AVC-coded images in one HEIF container (ISO/IEC 23008-12), used for bursts, animations and derived sequences rather than a single still.

It stands in the same relation to `image/avci` as [image/heic-sequence](/image/heic-sequence) does to [image/heic](/image/heic).

name: image/ktx
description:
KTX is the Khronos texture container: a thin wrapper around texture data that is already in a GPU-native compressed format, together with its mipmap chain, array layers and cube map faces.

The point is that the file needs no transcoding at load time. An engine reads the header, hands the payload straight to OpenGL or Vulkan, and the GPU consumes it as it stands — unlike [image/png](/image/png) or [image/jpeg](/image/jpeg), which must be decoded to raw pixels and then recompressed before they are useful as textures.

Version 2 is a separate media type, [image/ktx2](/image/ktx2).

name: image/ktx2
description:
KTX 2.0 is the second version of the Khronos texture container, and it addresses the problem that made [image/ktx](/image/ktx) awkward to ship: GPU texture formats are not portable, so a KTX 1 file had to be built per target platform.

KTX 2.0 adds Basis Universal supercompression, storing textures in an intermediate form that transcodes cheaply to whichever block format the device actually supports at load time. One file, every GPU.

glTF consumes it through the `KHR_texture_basisu` extension, which is where most people meet it.

name: image/vnd.valve.source.texture
description:
VTF is the texture format of Valve's Source engine — Half-Life 2, Portal, Team Fortress 2 and the games and mods built on them. A file holds the image data along with its mipmaps, flags and any animation frames the engine expects.

VTF files are almost always paired with a `.vmt` material script, which tells the engine which shader to use and how to interpret the texture. On its own a VTF is just pixels.

name: image/vnd.microsoft.icon
description:
The Windows icon format. An ICO file is a container: it holds several complete images at different sizes and colour depths, and the consumer picks whichever fits the space it needs to fill. That is how one `favicon.ico` serves both a 16-pixel browser tab and a 48-pixel desktop shortcut.

Images inside are stored either as BMP data or, since Windows Vista, as [image/png](/image/png).

Note the labelling mess: `image/vnd.microsoft.icon` is the registered type, but browsers and web servers overwhelmingly send [image/x-icon](/image/x-icon) instead. Both work in practice.

name: image/emf
description:
EMF, the Enhanced Metafile format, records a drawing as a replayable list of Windows GDI calls rather than as pixels — lines, curves, text and fills that scale cleanly to any resolution. It is registered by RFC 7903 and documented publicly as `[MS-EMF]`.

It is what lands on the clipboard when vector artwork is copied between Windows applications, and what Office embeds when a chart or diagram is pasted into a document.

RFC 7903 also records `image/x-emf` as deprecated in favour of this type.

name: image/wmf
description:
WMF is the original Windows Metafile format, the 16-bit predecessor to [image/emf](/image/emf), dating back to Windows 3.x. Like EMF it stores a sequence of GDI drawing commands rather than a bitmap, so the output scales, but the older record set is considerably more limited.

It is registered by RFC 7903 and documented as `[MS-WMF]`. You still find it inside older Office documents and clip-art libraries.

RFC 7903 also records `image/x-wmf` as deprecated in favour of this type.

name: image/dpx
description:
DPX (Digital Picture Exchange, SMPTE ST 268-1) stores a single motion picture frame. A sequence is a directory of numbered files, one per frame, which is exactly how film scanners and digital intermediate pipelines hand work between tools.

The header carries the metadata a post-production facility needs — timecode, film edge codes, the transfer characteristic — and the pixel data is typically 10 bits per channel in a logarithmic encoding that preserves highlight detail the way a film negative does.

It began as an evolution of Kodak's Cineon format and remains the common currency for uncompressed frame interchange.

name: image/aces
description:
The ACES image container file layout, standardised as SMPTE ST 2065-4. It is a constrained profile of OpenEXR: the same file structure, with colour space, channel naming and required attributes pinned down so that any ACES-compliant tool interprets the contents identically.

That constraint is the entire point. ACES exists to make colour behave predictably as footage moves between facilities, and a container that permits fewer choices is easier to be strict about.

Watch the extension. Files use `.exr`, the same as ordinary OpenEXR images, so the extension alone will not tell you whether a file follows the ACES profile.

name: image/vnd.radiance
description:
Radiance HDR, commonly called RGBE after its encoding, stores high dynamic range images by giving each pixel three 8-bit mantissas and one shared 8-bit exponent. Four bytes per pixel covers a range of many orders of magnitude — enough to hold both deep shadow and direct sun in one image.

It came out of the Radiance lighting simulation package at Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory and became the common format for environment maps and image-based lighting in 3D rendering.

IANA registers no extension for it. `.hdr` is by far the most common, with `.pic`, `.rgbe` and `.xyze` also in use; `.pic` is badly ambiguous and worth avoiding.

name: image/fits
description:
FITS, the Flexible Image Transport System, is the standard data format of astronomy, registered by RFC 4047 and maintained by the International Astronomical Union. A file is a sequence of header-and-data units: a human-readable ASCII header of keyword and value pairs, followed by an n-dimensional array.

It is not really an image format. The array may be a photograph from a telescope, but it may equally be a spectrum, a data cube or a table, and the header carries the calibration and coordinate information needed to interpret it scientifically.

Backwards compatibility is a stated design principle — files written decades ago still read correctly, which matters when the observations cannot be repeated.

furtherReading.title: RFC 4047 - MIME Sub-type Registrations for FITS

name: image/tiff-fx
description:
TIFF-FX is the image format for internet fax, registered by RFC 3950 with the file format itself defined in RFC 3949. It is a constrained profile of [image/tiff](/image/tiff): a specific set of compression schemes, resolutions and tags that a receiving fax device is guaranteed to understand.

The profiles run from plain black and white at fax resolution up to JBIG and JPEG-coded colour. Restricting the parent format this way is what makes interoperability possible between devices that share nothing else.

It is the payload carried by the email-based fax profiles rather than a format anyone authors directly.

furtherReading.title: RFC 3950 - Tag Image File Format Fax eXtended (TIFF-FX)

name: image/t38
description:
T.38 is the ITU-T recommendation for carrying fax over IP networks in real time, and this media type, registered by RFC 3362, labels the image data within it.

Rather than digitising the fax tones as audio and hoping they survive transcoding, a T.38 gateway demodulates the fax at one end, sends the page data over IP, and remodulates it at the other. That is what makes faxing work over VoIP at all.

You will meet this type inside SIP session descriptions rather than as a file on disk.

furtherReading.title: RFC 3362 - Real-time Facsimile (T.38) - image/t38 MIME Sub-type Registration

name: image/dicom-rle
description:
The run-length encoding defined by the DICOM standard for medical images, specified in PS3.5 Annex G. It is a byte-oriented RLE scheme derived from PackBits, applied separately to each colour plane.

Lossless compression matters in diagnostic imaging, where an artefact could be read as pathology. RLE is the simplest of DICOM's lossless options: it achieves very little on photographic data, but works well on the large uniform regions typical of segmentation masks and some modalities.

Where stronger lossless compression is needed, [image/jls](/image/jls) is the usual alternative.

name: image/vnd.zbrush.pcx
description:
A Pixologic registration for the PCX files written by ZBrush, the digital sculpting application. PCX itself is a much older ZSoft format from the DOS era, covered on this site at [image/x-pcx](/image/x-pcx).

The registration exists to give ZBrush's variant its own label. Public documentation of how it differs from ordinary PCX is thin, so treat the distinction as a vendor claim rather than a described format difference.

The practical consequence is the extension clash: a `.pcx` file may be either, and the extension alone will not tell you which.

name: audio/3gpp
description:
The 3GP container is the multimedia file format 3GPP defined for mobile networks, registered by RFC 3839 and specified in 3GPP TS 26.244. It is a variant of the ISO base media file format, the same structure underneath MP4, trimmed to the codecs handsets were expected to carry.

`audio/3gpp` labels a 3GP file whose contents are audio only, most often AMR or AMR-WB speech from a phone's voice recorder. The same container holding video as well is [video/3gpp](/video/3gpp).

The counterpart from the CDMA2000 side of the industry is [audio/3gpp2](/audio/3gpp2).

furtherReading.title: RFC 3839 - MIME Type Registrations for 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Multimedia files

name: audio/32kadpcm
description:
32 kbit/s ADPCM is the toll-quality speech coding of ITU-T G.726, registered as a media type by RFC 3802 after first appearing in the voice profile for internet mail in RFC 2421. Adaptive differential PCM codes the difference between successive samples rather than the samples themselves, halving the bitrate of G.711 with no perceptible loss on speech.

It is the coding behind voice messaging systems of that era. The `.726` extension names the ITU-T recommendation rather than the media type.

ADPCM in a RIFF wrapper is [audio/adpcm](/audio/adpcm).

furtherReading.title: RFC 3802 - Toll Quality Voice - 32 kbit/s Adaptive Differential Pulse Code Modulation (ADPCM) MIME Sub-type Registration

name: audio/amr
description:
AMR (Adaptive Multi-Rate) is the narrowband speech codec 3GPP adopted for GSM and UMTS telephony. RFC 4867 registers both its file storage format and its RTP payload format. It codes 8 kHz speech at eight bitrates between 4.75 and 12.2 kbit/s and moves between them as radio conditions change.

Voice recorder apps on feature phones wrote `.amr` files by the million, which is why the extension long outlived the networks it was designed for. The wideband version is [audio/amr-wb](/audio/amr-wb).

IANA spells this type `audio/AMR`. Media type names are case-insensitive under RFC 2045 section 5.1, so the lowercase form used here is the same type.

furtherReading.title: RFC 4867 - RTP Payload Format and File Storage Format for the Adaptive Multi-Rate (AMR) and Adaptive Multi-Rate Wideband (AMR-WB) Audio Codecs

name: audio/amr-wb
description:
AMR-WB (Adaptive Multi-Rate Wideband) extends AMR to a 16 kHz sampling rate, roughly doubling the coded bandwidth. It is standardised as ITU-T G.722.2 and 3GPP TS 26.190, and shares RFC 4867 with narrowband AMR for its storage and RTP payload formats.

That extra bandwidth is what stops a call sounding like a telephone, and it is the codec behind most first-generation HD Voice. Its successor in 3GPP is [audio/evs](/audio/evs).

IANA spells this type `audio/AMR-WB`. Media type names are case-insensitive under RFC 2045 section 5.1, so the lowercase form used here is the same type.

furtherReading.title: RFC 4867 - RTP Payload Format and File Storage Format for the Adaptive Multi-Rate (AMR) and Adaptive Multi-Rate Wideband (AMR-WB) Audio Codecs

name: audio/asc
description:
An `audio/asc` object is a bare AudioSpecificConfig, the MPEG-4 Audio structure that tells a decoder which coding tool, sampling rate and channel layout a stream uses. RFC 6295 registered it so that configuration could be fetched separately rather than carried inline with the audio.

Its only defined use is configuring an `audio/mpeg4-generic` RTP stream in rtp-midi mode, which is why it travels over HTTP or SMTP rather than sitting in a media file.

The registration gives `.acn` as the file extension, not `.asc`.

furtherReading.title: RFC 6295 - RTP Payload Format for MIDI

name: audio/atrac3
description:
ATRAC3 is the third generation of Sony's Adaptive TRansform Acoustic Coding, the family that started in MiniDisc. It codes stereo at 66, 105 or 132 kbit/s and carried Sony's Connect music store, the Walkman line and the PSP.

RFC 5584 defines the RTP payload format for the whole ATRAC family and registers this media type. The later variants are [audio/atrac-x](/audio/atrac-x) and [audio/atrac-advanced-lossless](/audio/atrac-advanced-lossless).

IANA spells this type `audio/ATRAC3`. Media type names are case-insensitive under RFC 2045 section 5.1, so the lowercase form used here is the same type.

furtherReading.title: RFC 5584 - RTP Payload Format for the Adaptive TRansform Acoustic Coding (ATRAC) Family

name: audio/atrac-advanced-lossless
description:
ATRAC Advanced Lossless stores a lossy ATRAC stream together with a correction layer that restores the original samples exactly. A player that understands only the lossy part still decodes the file; one that understands all of it reconstructs the source bit for bit.

That hybrid let a single file serve both a portable player and an archive copy. RFC 5584 registers it with the rest of the ATRAC family, alongside [audio/atrac3](/audio/atrac3) and [audio/atrac-x](/audio/atrac-x).

IANA spells this type `audio/ATRAC-ADVANCED-LOSSLESS`. Media type names are case-insensitive under RFC 2045 section 5.1, so the lowercase form used here is the same type.

furtherReading.title: RFC 5584 - RTP Payload Format for the Adaptive TRansform Acoustic Coding (ATRAC) Family

name: audio/atrac-x
description:
ATRAC-X is the media type for ATRAC3plus, Sony's revision of ATRAC3 that roughly doubles coding efficiency and stays usable near 64 kbit/s. It was the default on later Walkman players, the PSP and Hi-MD MiniDisc.

RFC 5584 defines the RTP payload format for the ATRAC family and registers this type. The earlier generation is [audio/atrac3](/audio/atrac3).

IANA spells this type `audio/ATRAC-X`. Media type names are case-insensitive under RFC 2045 section 5.1, so the lowercase form used here is the same type.

furtherReading.title: RFC 5584 - RTP Payload Format for the Adaptive TRansform Acoustic Coding (ATRAC) Family

name: audio/dls
description:
DLS (Downloadable Sounds) is the MIDI Manufacturers Association format for shipping the instrument samples a MIDI sequence expects, so a score is not left to whatever synthesiser the playback device happens to have. RFC 4613 registers the media type.

A DLS file holds wavetable samples together with the articulation data that maps them across the keyboard. Bundling one with a sequence for handsets is what [audio/mobile-xmf](/audio/mobile-xmf) does.

furtherReading.title: RFC 4613 - Media Type Registrations for Downloadable Sounds for Musical Instrument Digital Interface (MIDI)

name: audio/evrc
description:
EVRC (Enhanced Variable Rate Codec) is the CDMA speech codec 3GPP2 standardised as C.S0014. It picks a rate frame by frame between full, half and eighth rate, spending bits on speech and almost none on silence, which is how CDMA networks fitted more calls onto a carrier.

RFC 4788 registers the storage format for the EVRC family. Its later members are [audio/evrcb](/audio/evrcb), [audio/evrcwb](/audio/evrcwb) and [audio/evrcnw](/audio/evrcnw).

IANA spells this type `audio/EVRC`. Media type names are case-insensitive under RFC 2045 section 5.1, so the lowercase form used here is the same type.

furtherReading.title: RFC 4788 - Enhancements to RTP Payload Formats for EVRC Family Codecs

name: audio/evrc-qcp
description:
This is EVRC speech stored in QCP, the RIFF-based file format Qualcomm defined for vocoder data. RFC 3625 registers QCP together with the media types for the codecs carried inside it.

QCP is how CDMA handsets saved voice memos and how vocoder test vectors were exchanged. The bare storage format without the wrapper is [audio/evrc](/audio/evrc), and the same wrapper around the SMV vocoder is [audio/smv-qcp](/audio/smv-qcp).

IANA spells this type `audio/EVRC-QCP`. Media type names are case-insensitive under RFC 2045 section 5.1, so the lowercase form used here is the same type.

furtherReading.title: RFC 3625 - The QCP File Format and Media Types for Speech Data

name: audio/evrcb
description:
EVRC-B is the second generation of the CDMA Enhanced Variable Rate Codec, standardised by 3GPP2 as C.S0014-B. It keeps the variable-rate structure of the original but adds finer control over the average rate, so an operator can trade capacity against voice quality across a wider range.

RFC 5188 registers this media type alongside the wideband EVRC-WB. The narrowband original is [audio/evrc](/audio/evrc).

IANA spells this type `audio/EVRCB`. Media type names are case-insensitive under RFC 2045 section 5.1, so the lowercase form used here is the same type.

furtherReading.title: RFC 5188 - RTP Payload Format for the Enhanced Variable Rate Wideband Codec (EVRC-WB) and the Media Subtype Updates for EVRC-B Codec

name: audio/evrcnw
description:
EVRC-NW is the narrowband-wideband member of the CDMA EVRC family from 3GPP2. One stream can carry narrowband or wideband frames and switch between them mid-call, so a handset moving through changing coverage degrades smoothly instead of being handed to a different codec.

RFC 6884 defines its RTP payload format and registers this media type. It follows [audio/evrcb](/audio/evrcb) and [audio/evrcwb](/audio/evrcwb).

IANA spells this type `audio/EVRCNW`. Media type names are case-insensitive under RFC 2045 section 5.1, so the lowercase form used here is the same type.

furtherReading.title: RFC 6884 - RTP Payload Format for the Enhanced Variable Rate Narrowband-Wideband Codec (EVRC-NW)

name: audio/evrcwb
description:
EVRC-WB is the wideband member of the CDMA EVRC family, taking the codec to a 16 kHz sampling rate for noticeably clearer speech than the narrowband original. It is standardised by 3GPP2 as C.S0014-C.

RFC 5188 defines its RTP payload format and registers this media type, and in the same document updates the subtypes for EVRC-B. The narrowband original is [audio/evrc](/audio/evrc).

IANA spells this type `audio/EVRCWB`. Media type names are case-insensitive under RFC 2045 section 5.1, so the lowercase form used here is the same type.

furtherReading.title: RFC 5188 - RTP Payload Format for the Enhanced Variable Rate Wideband Codec (EVRC-WB) and the Media Subtype Updates for EVRC-B Codec

name: audio/evs
description:
EVS (Enhanced Voice Services) is the 3GPP codec introduced in Release 12 for voice over LTE, specified in 3GPP TS 26.441 and TS 26.445. It covers narrowband through fullband speech at rates from 5.9 to 128 kbit/s, and unlike earlier telephony codecs it handles music without falling apart.

It carries most VoLTE HD Voice, and includes an AMR-WB interoperable mode so calls reaching older networks need no transcoding. Its predecessor is [audio/amr-wb](/audio/amr-wb).

IANA spells this type `audio/EVS`. Media type names are case-insensitive under RFC 2045 section 5.1, so the lowercase form used here is the same type.

name: audio/ilbc
description:
iLBC (internet Low Bitrate Codec) codes narrowband speech at 13.33 or 15.2 kbit/s in independent frames. Because no frame depends on the one before it, a lost packet damages only what it carried instead of corrupting the decoder state that follows, which made it a common choice for VoIP over lossy links.

RFC 3952 defines its RTP payload format and registers this media type; the codec itself is specified in RFC 3951. The general-purpose codec that replaced it is [audio/opus](/audio/opus).

IANA spells this type `audio/iLBC`. Media type names are case-insensitive under RFC 2045 section 5.1, so the lowercase form used here is the same type.

furtherReading.title: RFC 3952 - Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) Payload Format for internet Low Bit Rate Codec (iLBC) Speech

name: audio/l16
description:
L16 is uncompressed 16-bit linear PCM, big-endian, as carried in the RTP profile for audio and video conferences. RFC 4856 registers it with the other payload formats in that profile. It defaults to 8 kHz mono, with rate and channel count set by media type parameters rather than by any header inside the data.

There is no container here at all: the payload is nothing but samples. PCM wrapped with a header that describes it is [audio/vnd.wav](/audio/vnd.wav).

IANA spells this type `audio/L16`. Media type names are case-insensitive under RFC 2045 section 5.1, so the lowercase form used here is the same type.

furtherReading.title: RFC 4856 - Media Type Registration of Payload Formats in the RTP Profile for Audio and Video Conferences

name: audio/matroska
description:
Matroska is the open container format specified by RFC 9559, built on EBML, a binary encoding that behaves like a typed and length-prefixed XML. `audio/matroska` labels a Matroska file holding audio only, conventionally saved as `.mka`.

The container is codec-agnostic and carries chapters, attachments and any number of selectable tracks, which is why WebM was derived from it. Before RFC 9559 gave it a registration the format circulated as [audio/x-matroska](/audio/x-matroska).

furtherReading.title: RFC 9559 - Matroska Media Container Format Specification

name: audio/mhas
description:
MHAS (MPEG-H Audio Stream) is the self-contained packet format for MPEG-H 3D Audio, defined in ISO/IEC 23008-3. Each stream carries the configuration needed to decode it alongside the audio itself, so a receiver can join partway through without a separate setup channel.

That property is why MHAS is the form MPEG-H takes in broadcast, where it provides next-generation audio for ATSC 3.0 and DVB. The same content packaged in an MP4 container is [audio/mp4](/audio/mp4).

name: audio/midi-clip
description:
A MIDI Clip File carries MIDI 2.0 data, the first substantial revision to MIDI since 1983. MIDI 2.0 widens 7-bit values to as much as 32 bits, adds per-note controllers, and makes the protocol bidirectional so devices can negotiate what they support instead of assuming.

The MIDI Association specifies the format as M2-116-U, version 1.0 of June 2023. It uses the `.midi2` extension to keep it distinct from the original [audio/midi](/audio/midi).

name: audio/mobile-xmf
description:
Mobile XMF is a profile of the Extensible Music Format aimed at handsets, registered by RFC 4723. XMF packages a MIDI sequence together with the DLS instrument bank it expects into one file, so a ringtone sounds the same everywhere rather than depending on each device's built-in synthesiser.

That bundling is the entire point of the format. The two parts it contains are [audio/midi](/audio/midi) and [audio/dls](/audio/dls).

furtherReading.title: RFC 4723 - Registration of Media Type audio/mobile-xmf

name: audio/prs.sid
description:
A PSID file holds music for the SID chip, the three-voice synthesiser in the Commodore 64. Instead of sampled audio it stores the 6502 machine code that drives the chip's registers, so playing one means emulating the processor and the SID together.

That is why a few kilobytes can hold several minutes of music, and why the tens of thousands of tunes collected by the demoscene remain playable today. The type sits in IANA's personal tree, which is what the `prs.` prefix marks.

furtherReading.title: SIDPLAY documentation - sidtune file formats (Internet Archive, 2001)

name: audio/smv
description:
SMV (Selectable Mode Vocoder) is the CDMA speech codec 3GPP2 standardised as C.S0030. Its design goal was to let an operator choose a working point between network capacity and voice quality by selecting one of several modes, rather than committing to one trade at deployment time.

RFC 3558 defines the RTP payload format for SMV and for the EVRC codecs, and registers this media type. Wrapped in Qualcomm's QCP file format it becomes [audio/smv-qcp](/audio/smv-qcp).

IANA spells this type `audio/SMV`. Media type names are case-insensitive under RFC 2045 section 5.1, so the lowercase form used here is the same type.

furtherReading.title: RFC 3558 - RTP Payload Format for Enhanced Variable Rate Codecs (EVRC) and Selectable Mode Vocoders (SMV)

name: audio/smv-qcp
description:
This is SMV speech stored in QCP, the RIFF-based container Qualcomm defined for vocoder data, registered by RFC 3625 along with the other codecs carried in it.

The `.qcp` extension is shared with [audio/evrc-qcp](/audio/evrc-qcp), because the wrapper is identical and only the vocoder inside differs. The bare SMV storage format is [audio/smv](/audio/smv).

IANA spells this type `audio/SMV-QCP`. Media type names are case-insensitive under RFC 2045 section 5.1, so the lowercase form used here is the same type.

furtherReading.title: RFC 3625 - The QCP File Format and Media Types for Speech Data

name: audio/sofa
description:
SOFA (Spatially Oriented Format for Acoustics) stores head-related transfer functions and room impulse responses: measurements of how a sound changes on its way to a listener depending on the direction it came from. Binaural renderers read them to place a sound in space over ordinary headphones.

The format is standardised as AES69 and built on netCDF, so a file carries self-describing multidimensional arrays together with the geometry of the measurement rig that produced them.

name: audio/sp-midi
description:
Scalable Polyphony MIDI constrains General MIDI so a sequence degrades predictably on a device that cannot sound every voice at once. The composer marks which notes matter most, and a synthesiser short of polyphony drops the others in a defined order instead of arbitrarily.

It was written for mobile phones, and the MIDI Manufacturers Association specifies it as RP-034, published December 2001. It shares the `.mid` extension with ordinary [audio/midi](/audio/midi).

name: audio/usac
description:
USAC (Unified Speech and Audio Coding) is defined in ISO/IEC 23003-3. It puts a speech coder and a general audio coder in one design and switches between them as the signal changes, so material mixing voice and music stays efficient instead of suffering whichever tool was the wrong choice.

Sold as xHE-AAC, it stays usable well below 32 kbit/s, which is why streaming services reach for it on low-bandwidth tiers. The registration gives `.loas` as the preferred extension. In an MP4 container the same coding appears as [audio/mp4](/audio/mp4).

name: text/vtt
description:
WebVTT (Web Video Text Tracks) is the W3C caption and subtitle format that the HTML `track` element loads. A file is plain UTF-8 text: the word `WEBVTT`, then cues giving a start time, an end time and the text to show between them.

Beyond captions it carries chapters, descriptions and arbitrary metadata cues, and cue settings can position text anywhere in the frame rather than only along the bottom. That range is why it displaced SRT on the web despite SRT being simpler to write.

furtherReading.title: W3C WebVTT: The Web Video Text Tracks Format

name: application/manifest+json
description:
A web app manifest is the JSON document that tells a browser how to install a site as an application: its name, icons, start URL, display mode and theme colour. The W3C Web Application Manifest specification defines it, and a page points at one with a `link` element whose `rel` is `manifest`.

It is what makes a Progressive Web App installable rather than merely bookmarkable. `.webmanifest` is the registered extension, though a great many sites serve the same document as `manifest.json`.

name: application/ld+json
description:
JSON-LD is JSON carrying a `@context` that maps its keys onto IRIs, so a document that reads like ordinary JSON also has machine-readable meaning. The W3C specifies it.

Most of the structured data on the web is JSON-LD inside a `script` element carrying this media type, describing a page's schema.org entities to search engines. Because the context does the linking, code that ignores it entirely still sees plain, readable JSON.

name: text/cache-manifest
description:
An application cache manifest listed the files a browser should retain for offline use. It arrived with HTML5 as AppCache, and both the W3C and browser vendors have since removed it.

It failed for a specific reason worth remembering: a manifest that could not be fetched left users pinned to stale files with no path back, and the update model gave a page no way to recover. Service workers replaced it. Files still exist in old projects, so the type is worth recognising, but nothing new should use it.

name: application/dash+xml
description:
An MPD (Media Presentation Description) is the manifest for MPEG-DASH, standardised as ISO/IEC 23009-1. It is an XML document listing the periods of a presentation, the adaptation sets within each, and the representations a player may choose between, with the URLs or byte ranges of every segment.

DASH is deliberately codec-agnostic, and the MPD is where that shows: a player reads it and switches representation as available bandwidth changes, without the format caring what codec sits inside.

name: text/wgsl
description:
WGSL (WebGPU Shading Language) is the shader language for WebGPU, specified by the W3C GPU for the Web working group. WebGPU accepts WGSL source directly rather than a compiled bytecode, so a `.wgsl` file is human-readable text that the browser compiles.

It exists because the web needed a shading language it could parse and validate itself, then translate safely to Direct3D, Metal and Vulkan, without trusting a binary from the page.

name: application/toml
description:
TOML (Tom's Obvious Minimal Language) is a configuration format designed to map unambiguously onto a hash table while staying obvious to read: sections in square brackets, `key = value` beneath them, and real types for strings, integers, dates and arrays.

Rust's `Cargo.toml` and Python's `pyproject.toml` are why most people meet it. Against YAML it trades expressiveness for predictability, since there is far less that can be written two different ways.

name: application/cbor
description:
CBOR (Concise Binary Object Representation) is a binary format defined by RFC 8949. It covers roughly JSON's data model and adds byte strings, unambiguous integers and floats, and an extension mechanism through numeric tags.

It is designed to be encoded and decoded without a schema and in very little code, which is why it turns up in constrained devices, in COSE for signing and encryption, and in WebAuthn attestation.

name: application/geo+json
description:
GeoJSON encodes geographic features as JSON, defined by RFC 7946. A document is a Feature or a FeatureCollection, and each feature pairs a geometry (Point, LineString, Polygon, or their multi- forms) with arbitrary properties.

RFC 7946 pinned the coordinate reference system to WGS 84 with longitude before latitude. That single decision removed the largest source of disagreement between implementations of the earlier community specification.

name: application/json-patch+json
description:
JSON Patch describes a change to a JSON document, defined by RFC 6902. A patch is an array of operations, each naming one of add, remove, replace, move, copy or test and pointing at a location with a JSON Pointer.

Sent as the body of an HTTP PATCH it lets a client alter one field without transmitting or overwriting the whole resource. The `test` operation is what makes an update safely conditional: if the document is not in the expected state the patch fails rather than silently clobbering a concurrent edit.

name: application/node
description:
This type labels JavaScript intended to run as a Node.js CommonJS module rather than to be delivered to a browser. The registration is maintained by the Node.js Technical Steering Committee.

The registration is candid about the overlap. It notes that the type "occupies the same file extension as other media types", and that a `.js` file "should be considered ambiguous if the intended execution environment is unknown". Server-side and browser JavaScript share the extension, and a web server should still send [text/javascript](/text/javascript).

name: application/sql
description:
RFC 6922 registers this type so that a file of SQL statements can be labelled as such in transit. The registration deliberately says nothing about which dialect the statements are written in.

That silence matters in practice. A dump from PostgreSQL, from MySQL and from SQLite all carry this same type, and none of them will load into the others unedited. The type tells you the file is SQL, not that your database can read it. The unregistered spelling still in common use is [application/x-sql](/application/x-sql).

name: application/x-sql
description:
This is the unregistered form of the SQL media type, and the one more likely to appear in the wild. It was in use before RFC 6922 registered [application/sql](/application/sql) and carried on afterwards, as `x-` types generally do.

Neither form replaces the other. Tools emit whichever they were written against, and both mean the same thing: a file of SQL statements whose dialect is not stated anywhere in the label.

furtherReading.title: Let's Solve the File Format Problem!

name: application/zstd
description:
Zstandard is a lossless compression format defined by RFC 8878. At its default setting it reaches roughly gzip's ratio several times faster, and at high settings it compresses considerably harder than gzip can.

Its distinguishing feature is the trained dictionary. Given a sample of the small documents you mean to compress, it derives a dictionary that lets each one compress well despite being far too small for the algorithm to find redundancy in on its own.

furtherReading.title: RFC 8878 - Zstandard Compression and the 'application/zstd' Media Type

name: application/sarif+json
description:
SARIF (Static Analysis Results Interchange Format) is the OASIS standard for reporting what a code analysis tool found. A run records the tool, the rules it applied, and every result with its location, severity and enough surrounding context to be understood without rerunning the tool.

It exists so that every linter and scanner stops inventing its own output format. GitHub code scanning consumes SARIF, which is most of why analysis tools now emit it alongside whatever they produced before.

name: application/spdx+json
description:
SPDX (Software Package Data Exchange) is the Linux Foundation's standard for describing what a software release contains: its packages, their versions and licences, and the relationships between them. This type is the JSON serialisation of an SPDX document.

It is one of the formats accepted as a software bill of materials, which is what moved SPDX from a licence-compliance tool into something shipped alongside releases and checked by procurement.

name: application/vnd.mermaid
description:
Mermaid diagrams are written as plain text and rendered to SVG, so a flowchart or sequence diagram lives in version control and is reviewed as a diff rather than as an opaque attachment that has to be opened.

The syntax is line-oriented: name the diagram type, then declare nodes and the edges between them. Built-in rendering in GitHub and GitLab markdown is why it spread beyond its own tooling.

name: application/vnd.apache.parquet
description:
Parquet is the Apache Software Foundation's columnar storage format. Values from a single column are stored together, so a query touching three columns out of two hundred reads only those three, and each column compresses well because everything in it is alike.

A file also carries its own schema and per-column statistics, letting a reader skip entire row groups that cannot satisfy a predicate. That combination is why it became the default for analytical data at rest. Where Parquet optimises storage, [application/vnd.apache.arrow.file](/application/vnd.apache.arrow.file) optimises handoff.

name: application/vnd.apache.arrow.file
description:
Arrow's IPC file format writes a columnar table to disk with a footer holding the schema and the position of every record batch, so a reader can seek directly to any batch instead of scanning from the start.

The point is Arrow's in-memory layout. Because the file holds the same representation the library already uses in memory, reading is closer to mapping than to parsing. The form without a footer, for pipes and sockets, is [application/vnd.apache.arrow.stream](/application/vnd.apache.arrow.stream).

name: application/vnd.apache.arrow.stream
description:
This is the streaming form of Arrow's IPC format: a schema message followed by record batches, written and read strictly in order, with no footer at the end.

Having no footer means there is nothing to seek to, so a consumer cannot jump to the tenth batch. It also means the stream does not have to exist in full before reading starts, which is what makes this the right choice over a socket or a pipe, where the random access of [application/vnd.apache.arrow.file](/application/vnd.apache.arrow.file) was never available anyway.

name: text/vcard
description:
vCard is the contact format defined by RFC 6350, which specifies version 4.0. A card is a run of properties such as FN, TEL, EMAIL and ADR between `BEGIN:VCARD` and `END:VCARD` lines, and one file may hold many cards in sequence.

It is what an address book exports and what a phone attaches when someone shares a contact. The registration lists both extensions, but `.vcf` is the one almost every implementation actually writes.

name: text/xml
description:
RFC 7303 registers `text/xml` alongside `application/xml` for XML documents. The two are functionally equivalent, and the RFC recommends [application/xml](/application/xml) for general use.

The distinction is historical. A `text/` type once implied the content was readable without special tooling, and the two types also differed in how a missing charset parameter was interpreted. RFC 7303 settled that: both now default the same way, leaving little reason to prefer this spelling beyond the many servers already sending it.

name: application/vnd.api+json
description:
JSON:API is a convention for building JSON APIs. It fixes how resources, relationships, pagination, filtering, sparse field selection and errors are shaped, so those decisions stop being renegotiated on every project.

The media type is part of the specification rather than incidental to it. A server signals JSON:API semantics by sending this type, and content negotiation on it is how a client asks for them, which is why the type matters more here than for most JSON formats.

name: text/x-opml
description:
OPML (Outline Processor Markup Language) is an XML format for nested outlines. Its dominant use by a wide margin is exchanging feed subscription lists: nearly every feed reader imports and exports OPML, which is what makes moving between readers possible at all.

There is no IANA registration, so the `x-` form is what tools send and expect. The outline structure itself is generic, and a few outliners and mind-mapping tools use it for its original purpose.

furtherReading.title: Let's Solve the File Format Problem!

name: model/gltf+json
description:
glTF (GL Transmission Format) is the Khronos Group's runtime format for 3D scenes and models. It is built for delivery rather than authoring: a file holds the scene graph, materials and animations, and points at binary buffers of geometry that an engine can hand to the GPU with almost no processing.

That focus on load time is why it gets called the JPEG of 3D. This type is the JSON form, which references its buffers and textures as separate files. Everything packed into a single binary container is [model/gltf-binary](/model/gltf-binary).

name: model/gltf-binary
description:
GLB is the single-file form of glTF: the same JSON scene description, with its binary buffers and textures packed into one container behind a short header. Nothing has to be fetched separately, which makes it the practical choice for shipping a model over a network.

Textures inside a GLB are often Basis Universal supercompressed and carried as [image/ktx2](/image/ktx2), through the KHR_texture_basisu extension. The form that keeps its buffers as separate files is [model/gltf+json](/model/gltf+json).

name: model/obj
description:
The Wavefront OBJ format dates from the Advanced Visualizer in 1992 and has outlived that software by three decades. It is plain text: vertex positions, texture coordinates and normals, then the faces that index them, one declaration per line.

Its longevity comes from that simplicity. Almost every 3D tool reads it and a person can inspect one in a text editor. Surface appearance is not in the file at all; it lives in a companion [model/mtl](/model/mtl) named by an `mtllib` line.

furtherReading.title: Library of Congress - Wavefront OBJ File Format

name: model/mtl
description:
An MTL file holds the material definitions that an [model/obj](/model/obj) file refers to: ambient, diffuse and specular colours, shininess, transparency and the paths of any texture maps.

Keeping them apart is deliberate, since geometry changes far less often than appearance does. Both formats were registered by the DICOM Standards Committee, which needed a way to label 3D manufacturing data carried alongside medical imaging.

name: model/3mf
description:
3MF (3D Manufacturing Format) is the 3MF Consortium's format for additive manufacturing. A `.3mf` file is a ZIP archive of XML parts describing the model together with materials, colours, print tickets and slice data.

It exists because STL carries triangles and nothing else: no units, no colour, no materials, no metadata, leaving every toolchain to guess at the rest. Related: [model/stl](/model/stl).

name: model/step
description:
STEP (Standard for the Exchange of Product model data) is the ISO 10303 family, the neutral format CAD systems use to exchange solid models without passing through a vendor's own kernel. A STEP file carries exact boundary representation geometry rather than a triangle mesh, so a curved surface stays curved.

This type covers the Part 21 clear-text encoding. The same encoding registered in the application tree is [application/p21](/application/p21). The XML and zipped forms are [model/step+xml](/model/step+xml), [model/step+zip](/model/step+zip) and [model/step-xml+zip](/model/step-xml+zip).

name: model/step+xml
description:
This is STEP product data in the XML encoding of ISO 10303-28, rather than the Part 21 clear text that most CAD tools write.

XML makes the data reachable with ordinary tooling, at a considerable cost in file size. That cost is why the compressed variants exist: [model/step-xml+zip](/model/step-xml+zip) is this encoding zipped, and [model/step+zip](/model/step+zip) is the clear-text form zipped. The uncompressed clear-text encoding is [model/step](/model/step).

name: model/step+zip
description:
A ZIP archive containing a STEP Part 21 file, registered so that a compressed exchange package carries a type describing what is inside rather than being labelled as a generic archive.

STEP files for a full assembly routinely reach hundreds of megabytes of clear text, which compresses by roughly an order of magnitude, so the zipped form is how large models actually move between organisations. The uncompressed form is [model/step](/model/step), and the zipped XML encoding is [model/step-xml+zip](/model/step-xml+zip).

name: model/step-xml+zip
description:
A ZIP archive containing STEP data in the ISO 10303-28 XML encoding. It exists for the same reason as [model/step+zip](/model/step+zip): the payload is verbose text that compresses heavily.

The distinction between the two zipped types is only what sits inside the archive. This one holds the XML encoding, whose uncompressed form is [model/step+xml](/model/step+xml); the other holds Part 21 clear text.

name: application/p21
description:
ISO 10303-21 defines the clear-text encoding that STEP files use, commonly called Part 21. It is structured text: a header section, then a data section of numbered entity instances that refer to one another by those numbers.

The registration claims `.ifc` alongside the STEP extensions, which is correct rather than a stray entry. IFC, the schema behind building information modelling, is serialised with this same Part 21 syntax. The model-tree registration of the encoding is [model/step](/model/step), and the schema language that says what the numbered entities mean is [application/express](/application/express).

name: application/express
description:
EXPRESS is the data modelling language defined by ISO 10303-11. It is not product data itself: it is the language in which STEP's application protocols are written, describing entities, their attributes and the constraints between them.

A `.exp` file is therefore closer to a database schema than to a model. Reading one is how you find out what the numbered entities inside a [model/step](/model/step) or [application/p21](/application/p21) file actually represent.

name: model/vnd.usda
description:
USD (Universal Scene Description) is Pixar's system for composing large 3D scenes out of layers that reference and override one another, so many artists can work on one scene without ever editing the same file. This type is the human-readable ASCII form.

Being text, it can be diffed and edited by hand, which is why it is the form used for layer files that do composition work rather than for carrying heavy geometry. The packaged single-file form is [model/vnd.usdz+zip](/model/vnd.usdz+zip).

name: model/vnd.usdz+zip
description:
USDZ packages a USD scene together with its textures in a single ZIP, stored uncompressed and aligned so a reader can memory-map assets straight out of the archive without extracting anything first.

Leaving it uncompressed is the whole design: it trades file size for the ability to begin rendering immediately, which is what makes it Apple's format for AR Quick Look. The text form of the scene description itself is [model/vnd.usda](/model/vnd.usda).

name: model/x3d+xml
description:
X3D is the Web3D Consortium's successor to VRML, standardised as ISO/IEC 19775. This type is the XML encoding, which is the most common way X3D scenes are written and the one ordinary XML tooling can validate.

The registration sets a compression convention shared by every X3D encoding: append `z` to the extension when the file is GZIP compressed, so `.x3dz` is a gzipped `.x3d`. The other encodings are [model/x3d-vrml](/model/x3d-vrml) and [model/x3d+fastinfoset](/model/x3d+fastinfoset), and the format it succeeds is [model/vrml](/model/vrml).

name: model/x3d-vrml
description:
This is X3D written in the classic VRML syntax rather than XML, for tools and content carried forward from VRML. The scene graph is identical to the XML encoding; only the way it is written down differs.

Note the hyphen in the type name. It is `model/x3d-vrml`, not `x3d+vrml`: the `+suffix` convention is reserved for structured syntaxes such as XML or JSON, and the VRML classic encoding is not one of those. GZIP compressed, the extension becomes `.x3dvz`.

name: model/x3d+fastinfoset
description:
This is the binary encoding of X3D, using Fast Infoset (ISO/IEC 24824-1), a standardised binary serialisation of an XML infoset. The scene is the same as the XML form, but compact and quicker to parse.

Fast Infoset replaced an earlier binary proposal, which is why older material sometimes mentions a `model/x3d+binary` type. That name was never registered and resolves to nothing. GZIP compressed, this encoding uses `.x3dbz`. The text form is [model/x3d+xml](/model/x3d+xml).

name: model/u3d
description:
U3D (Universal 3D) is defined by ECMA-363, which ECMA publishes free of charge. It carries meshes, materials, lighting and animation in a compact binary form supporting progressive refinement, so a coarse version of a model can be shown while detail is still arriving.

Its main use today is 3D content embedded in PDF. A U3D stream, or a [model/prc](/model/prc) one, is what makes an interactive model inside a document possible.

name: model/prc
description:
PRC (Product Representation Compact) is defined by ISO 14739-1 and is the second format PDF supports for embedded 3D. Unlike a mesh format it can carry exact boundary representation geometry, so an engineering model keeps its true curved surfaces inside the document.

That is the difference from [model/u3d](/model/u3d). U3D is a visualisation format; PRC can hold the CAD data itself, which matters when the PDF is the deliverable for a part someone has to manufacture.

name: model/vnd.collada+xml
description:
COLLADA is Khronos's XML interchange format for 3D assets, intended to move a scene between digital content creation tools without either tool imposing its native format. A `.dae` file can hold geometry, materials, shaders, physics and animation.

It was the interchange standard of the 2000s and remains widely readable. For delivery to a runtime, as opposed to exchange between authoring tools, Khronos now points at [model/gltf+json](/model/gltf+json).

name: model/jt
description:
JT is the lightweight visualisation format used across automotive and aerospace engineering, standardised as ISO 14306. It carries tessellated geometry at several levels of detail, optionally alongside the exact boundary representation, so a design review can open a complete vehicle assembly without loading the full CAD model.

Selective loading is the point. A viewer fetches only the parts and the detail levels it currently needs, which is what makes assemblies of that size workable at all. Related: [model/step](/model/step).

IANA spells this type `model/JT`. Media type names are case-insensitive under RFC 2045 section 5.1, so the lowercase form used here is the same type.

name: model/vnd.opengex
description:
OpenGEX (Open Game Engine Exchange) is a text-based interchange format for game engine assets, carrying geometry, materials, animation and skinning in a structure meant to be read straight into an engine's own representation.

It was designed as a deliberate reaction to the complexity of COLLADA, aiming at a format an engine could import without pulling in a large library. Related: [model/vnd.collada+xml](/model/vnd.collada+xml).

name: application/problem+json
description:
A problem details object is the standard shape for an HTTP error body, defined by RFC 9457. Instead of inventing a JSON envelope per API, a response carries `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail` and `instance`, where `type` is a URI naming the kind of problem so a client can branch on it without reading prose.

RFC 9457 replaced RFC 7807, adding a registry of common problem type URIs and guidance for type URIs that cannot be dereferenced. The same model serialised as XML is [application/problem+xml](/application/problem+xml).

furtherReading.title: RFC 9457 - Problem Details for HTTP APIs

name: application/problem+xml
description:
The XML serialisation of the problem details model from RFC 9457, the standard shape for an HTTP error body. It carries the same members as the JSON form, `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail` and `instance`, as child elements of a `problem` element in the `urn:ietf:rfc:7807` namespace.

That namespace still names the older specification, because RFC 9457 kept it unchanged when it replaced RFC 7807. Most APIs reach for [application/problem+json](/application/problem+json); this exists so an XML API does not have to invent an error format of its own.

furtherReading.title: RFC 9457 - Problem Details for HTTP APIs

name: application/merge-patch+json
description:
JSON Merge Patch, defined by RFC 7396, describes a change to a JSON document by sending something that looks like the document. Members in the patch replace the ones they match, a member set to `null` is removed, and anything left out is untouched.

That shape is easy to write and easy to get wrong. It cannot address a single array element, cannot express a precondition, and has no way to set a member to `null`, because `null` already means delete. When any of that matters, [application/json-patch+json](/application/json-patch+json) spells each operation out instead.

name: application/json-seq
description:
A JSON text sequence is any number of JSON values in one stream, each preceded by an ASCII record separator (0x1E) and followed by a line feed, as defined by RFC 7464. The separator cannot appear unescaped inside a JSON text, so a reader can always find where the next value starts.

That suits a long or never-ending sequence that would be awkward as a single enormous array: a consumer handles each value as it arrives instead of waiting for a closing bracket, and one malformed value need not be fatal. `jq` reads and writes it with the `--seq` flag.

furtherReading.title: RFC 7464 - JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Text Sequences

name: application/jsonpath
description:
JSONPath selects values out of a JSON document. An expression starts at the root `$` and applies segments, so `$.store.book[*].author` picks the author of every book and `$..price` finds every price at any depth.

The syntax began as Stefan Gössner's 2007 proposal and spread through dozens of libraries long before anyone wrote it down, which left implementations quietly incompatible with each other. RFC 9535 is the specification that fixes that, and this media type is registered for carrying a query, not the values it returns.

furtherReading.title: RFC 9535 - JSONPath: Query Expressions for JSON

name: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
description:
This is what an HTML form posts by default: each name and value percent-encoded, pairs joined with `&`, name separated from value by `=`, and a space written as `+`. It is older than most of this list and is specified today in the WHATWG URL Standard rather than in HTML itself.

The `+` is the part that catches people out, since percent-encoding elsewhere writes a space as `%20`. The format also has no way to carry a file, which is what multipart/form-data exists for. Its registration gives no file extension, because it only ever appears on the wire.

name: application/http
description:
This type carries one or more complete HTTP request or response messages as a payload, registered in Section 10.2 of RFC 9112. The `msgtype` parameter says whether the enclosed messages are requests or responses, and `version` gives the HTTP version, though a reader can work both out from the first line.

It exists so HTTP messages can travel through something that is not an HTTP connection: batched into one request, stored, or attached to a report. [message/rfc822](/message/rfc822) does the equivalent job for a single email message.

name: application/scim+json
description:
SCIM, the System for Cross-domain Identity Management, is the protocol an identity provider uses to create, update and deactivate accounts in another service. RFC 7644 defines it, and this type marks its JSON payloads: users, groups, and the schema documents that describe what a resource may contain.

It is what sits behind automated user provisioning in enterprise single sign-on. The registration notes that older SCIM deployments send plain [application/json](/application/json) instead, so a server that wants to interoperate widely usually accepts both.

furtherReading.title: RFC 7644 - System for Cross-domain Identity Management: Protocol

name: application/linkset
description:
A linkset is a collection of web links published as its own document rather than crammed into an HTTP `Link` header. RFC 9264 defines it, and this form reuses the exact field syntax of that header, from RFC 8288, so the same text can be moved out of the response headers and served as a resource.

Header size is limited and links are sometimes numerous, which is the whole reason the format exists: a resource can point at its linkset instead of carrying every link on every response. The JSON serialisation is [application/linkset+json](/application/linkset+json).

furtherReading.title: RFC 9264 - Linkset: Media Types and a Link Relation Type for Link Sets

name: application/linkset+json
description:
The JSON serialisation of a linkset, a set of web links served as a document instead of squeezed into an HTTP `Link` header. RFC 9264 defines both forms. This one is an object whose sole member, `linkset`, holds an array of link context objects, each with an optional `anchor` and then one member per relation type listing the targets.

Most clients would rather parse this than the header field syntax used by [application/linkset](/application/linkset), which is the other form the same specification defines. The registration proposes no extension beyond the generic `.json`.

furtherReading.title: RFC 9264 - Linkset: Media Types and a Link Relation Type for Link Sets

name: application/reputon+json
description:
A reputon is one reputation score about one thing, defined by RFC 7071. The object names the subject being rated, the application the rating belongs to, the assertion being made about it, and a rating expressed as a floating-point value between 0.0 and 1.0 inclusive.

The application name is what gives the number meaning, and each one is registered separately: RFC 7072 defines the email identifier application, which rates a sending domain. Little else adopted the format, but it is the standard answer to a question that most services still answer with a bespoke JSON object.

furtherReading.title: RFC 7071 - A Media Type for Reputation Interchange

name: application/expect-ct-report+json
description:
The Expect-CT response header let a site ask browsers to enforce Certificate Transparency, and to report any certificate for it that had not been properly logged. This type marks those reports, which the browser posted to the address the header named. RFC 9163 documents the header and the report format as an Experimental specification.
