The feature is finished. Only Chromium implemented it, and Chromium deprecated the header in version 107 on the grounds that it now enforces Certificate Transparency for every publicly trusted certificate anyway.

name: application/jwt
description:
A JSON Web Token is not a format of its own. It is a JWS or a JWE whose payload happens to be a JSON claims set, which is why the tokens people recognise are three base64url segments joined by dots. RFC 7519 defines the claims, `iss`, `sub`, `aud`, `exp` and the rest, rather than the container around them.

That relationship is the thing worth knowing, because verifying a JWT means verifying the JWS it arrived in. The generic type for that container, whatever its payload, is [application/jose](/application/jose), and the keys used to check the signature are published as [application/jwk-set+json](/application/jwk-set+json).

name: application/jose
description:
RFC 7515 registers this for content that is a JWS or a JWE in compact serialisation: base64url segments separated by dots, with nothing in the media type to say which of the two it is. Compact serialisation is the form that fits in a URL, a header or a cookie.

Use it when the payload is not a JSON claims set, because that case has its own name, [application/jwt](/application/jwt). The JSON serialisation of the same structures, which can carry more than one signature over a payload, is [application/jose+json](/application/jose+json).

name: application/jose+json
description:
The JSON serialisation of a JWS or a JWE, registered by RFC 7515 alongside the compact form. Instead of dot-separated segments it is an object, with the protected header, the payload and the signatures as named members.

The reason to reach for it is that this form can carry several signatures, or several recipients, over one payload. The compact form cannot express that at all. It is also bulkier and not safe to drop into a URL, which is why [application/jose](/application/jose) is what ends up in headers and cookies.

name: application/jwk+json
description:
A JSON Web Key is one cryptographic key written as a JSON object, defined by RFC 7517. The `kty` member says what kind of key it is and the rest follow from that: `n` and `e` for RSA, `crv`, `x` and `y` for an elliptic curve key. A `kid` names the key so a token can point at the one that signed it.

Putting keys in JSON is what made rotation ordinary on the web, because publishing a key became a matter of serving a document. The collection an endpoint actually publishes is [application/jwk-set+json](/application/jwk-set+json).

name: application/jwk-set+json
description:
A JWK Set is an object whose `keys` member holds an array of JSON Web Keys. RFC 7517 defines both, and this is the one a service publishes: the document behind a `jwks_uri` that lets anyone verify the tokens that service issues.

A set rather than a single key is what allows rotation without downtime. The issuer adds the new key beside the old one, starts signing with it, and removes the old one once the tokens it signed have expired. A verifier picks the right entry by matching the token's `kid`. One key on its own is [application/jwk+json](/application/jwk+json).

name: application/at+jwt
description:
RFC 9068 profiles the JWT for use as an OAuth 2.0 access token, so a resource server can validate a token by itself instead of asking the authorization server about it. The profile fixes which claims must be present and requires the token to be signed, ruling out the `none` algorithm.

The media type is the point of the profile, not a footnote to it. A conforming token must carry `at+jwt` in its `typ` header, which is what stops one kind of JWT being accepted where another was expected. Without that, an access token and an [application/jwt](/application/jwt) issued for some other purpose can look alike to a verifier.

furtherReading.title: RFC 9068 - JSON Web Token (JWT) Profile for OAuth 2.0 Access Tokens

name: application/secevent+jwt
description:
A Security Event Token reports that something happened, rather than asserting who someone is. RFC 8417 defines it as a JWT with an `events` claim, an object whose member names identify the event types, leaving a profile such as OpenID's Shared Signals to say what those types mean.

It is how an identity provider tells a relying party that an account was disabled or a session revoked, out of band from any sign-in. RFC 8417 devotes a section to keeping a SET from being mistaken for an ID token or an access token, and this media type is part of that answer.

name: application/token-introspection+jwt
description:
OAuth 2.0 token introspection normally answers with a plain JSON object. RFC 9701 defines a signed answer instead: the authorization server returns the response as a JWT, so the caller can tell who produced it and that nobody altered it in between.

The introspection members sit under a single `token_introspection` claim, deliberately kept apart from the JWT's own claims so that a name cannot mean two things in one document. That matters when the answer crosses a trust boundary, or when a resource server may later have to show what it was told. The token being described is often an [application/at+jwt](/application/at+jwt).

furtherReading.title: RFC 9701 - JSON Web Token (JWT) Response for OAuth Token Introspection

name: application/logout+jwt
description:
A Logout Token is what an OpenID Connect provider posts to each relying party when a user signs out, so that sessions elsewhere end too. It is a JWT carrying an `events` claim with the member name `http://schemas.openid.net/event/backchannel-logout`, and a `sub` or a `sid` saying whose session to end.

A `nonce` claim is prohibited, and the reason is worth reading twice: its absence makes a Logout Token syntactically invalid as an ID token, so a forged authentication response cannot pass one off as the other. The OpenID Foundation registered the type and its specification is public.

name: text/turtle
description:
Turtle is how most people actually write RDF. It is the W3C's compact text syntax for a graph: prefixes declared once with `@prefix`, `a` standing in for rdf:type, and semicolons and commas so one subject can carry many statements without being named again.

The RDF 1.1 Turtle Recommendation defines it, and it sits deliberately between two neighbours. Take every abbreviation out and what remains is [application/n-triples](/application/n-triples). Add named graphs and it becomes [application/trig](/application/trig). The XML serialisation that came first is [application/rdf+xml](/application/rdf+xml).

name: application/n-triples
description:
N-Triples is the line-based subset of Turtle: one statement per line, every term written out in full, no prefixes and no abbreviations at all. The W3C Recommendation calls it easy to parse, which is the entire design goal.

Being verbose to read is what makes it convenient for everything else. A file can be split at any newline, streamed, sorted, diffed or compared line by line, which is why a format invented for test cases became the usual way to ship bulk RDF. Add graph labels and it becomes [application/n-quads](/application/n-quads); add abbreviations and it becomes [text/turtle](/text/turtle).

name: application/trig
description:
TriG is Turtle extended to write down a complete RDF dataset rather than a single graph. Statements are grouped into named graphs, each introduced by the IRI naming it, alongside a default graph for anything left unattributed.

Named graphs are what let a store record where a statement came from, or when it was asserted, without altering the statement itself. Everything [text/turtle](/text/turtle) can express, TriG expresses the same way, so Turtle is the subset to reach for when one graph is all there is. The line-based form of the same dataset is [application/n-quads](/application/n-quads).

name: application/n-quads
description:
N-Quads is N-Triples with one more element on each line, an optional graph label after the object, which turns a file of statements into a whole RDF dataset. The W3C Recommendation puts it plainly: the main distinction from [application/n-triples](/application/n-triples) is that N-Quads can encode multiple graphs.

Everything that makes N-Triples convenient survives the addition. Each line still stands alone, so a dataset of any size can be streamed, sorted or split without a parser holding state. The readable form of the same dataset, with prefixes and grouping, is [application/trig](/application/trig).

name: text/n3
description:
Notation3 came first and Turtle is the part of it that stays inside RDF. What was left behind is the interesting half: N3 adds variables and implication, so a document can state a rule and not only a fact, and a reasoner can then derive conclusions nobody wrote down.

It also treats a graph as a term, which allows statements about statements. The registration cites the 2008 W3C Team Submission, while the language is now maintained by a W3C Community Group. Anything that only records facts is better written as [text/turtle](/text/turtle), which every RDF tool can read.

furtherReading.title: W3C Notation3 (N3): A readable RDF syntax

name: text/shaclc
description:
SHACL validates RDF graphs against shapes, and SHACL's own syntax is RDF, which makes a shapes file precise and tiring to read. The compact syntax is an alternative notation for a subset of SHACL Core, aimed at people editing shapes by hand.

It is not a second language. A compact document maps to the RDF form and back, so tools keep working. The specification began in the RDF Data Shapes Working Group and continues in the SHACL Community Group, so it is not a Recommendation. The other way to describe the shape of a graph, with a grammar of its own rather than a second syntax, is [text/shex](/text/shex).

name: text/shex
description:
Shape Expressions describe what an RDF graph has to look like: which properties a node carries, how many values each may have, and what those values must be in turn. This type names the compact syntax, which reads like a grammar; the same schema also has JSON and RDF forms.

ShEx and SHACL answer the same question and are easy to mix up. ShEx was built as a schema language with a notation of its own, developed in a W3C Community Group. SHACL is written in RDF and became a Recommendation, then added [text/shaclc](/text/shaclc) to solve the readability problem ShEx never had.
